qa.question:
FY2026 revenue was RM201.2 million, comprising RM123.2 million from progressive 
billings for properties under development and RM78.0 million from sales of completed 
inventories, including Vivo Executive Apartment and Viluxe Phase 1, and other revenue, 
including the sale of development land.  
 
(i) 
Versa: Of the 980 residential units, how many have been sold under binding 
sale and purchase agreements, and what is the percentage and total value of 
contracted sales against the project's gross development value (GDV) of 
RM429.1 million?  
 
(ii) 
Viluxe: Phase 1 of the project was completed in June 2024, with the certificate of 
completion and compliance obtained in May 2024. Against the projected GDV of 
RM396.9 million, what proportion of Phase 1's GDV has been secured 
through contracted sales and how many of the 174 units in Phase 1 remain 
unsold? What factors will determine when management proceeds with 
future phases? 
 
(iii) 
Sales progress disclosure: Will the board commit to disclosing, in future 
annual reports, the number of units sold, contracted sales value and sales 
progress by development? This would enable shareholders to assess demand 
and the group's exposure to unsold inventory. 
 
In addition, the group launched its first serviced apartment development in Aspen Vision 
City, Mezon @ Park Enclave, and finalised the masterplan for Rivanis. Developed in 
partnership with Kerjaya Prospek Group Berhad and in collaboration with Railway Assets 
Corporation (RAC), Rivanis is a transit-oriented, mixed-use development in Perai, Penang. 
 
(iv) 
Mezon @ Park Enclave: How many units have been sold under binding sale 
and purchase agreements, and how does this compare with management's 
initial sales expectations for the group’s first serviced apartment? What is 
the typical profile of the buyers?  
 
(v) 
Rivanis: With a 45% stake in the project, what capital commitments, 
development responsibilities and management resources will the group 
contribute? How will responsibilities be allocated among the partners, and 
what governance rights does the group have over key decisions, including 
project financing, budgets and development milestones?

Would the board/management provide shareholders with greater clarity on several 
financial and operational matters? Specifically:  

(Source: company annual report; emphasis added) 
 
(i) 
Can management provide a project-by-project breakdown of the 
impairment losses on development properties and development costs 
written off during FY2026, including the amount attributable to each 
project and the underlying reasons for the charges? 
 
Note 5 states that, as at 30 June 2026, the group held investment properties with a carrying 
value of RM35.2 million. These assets were transferred from property, plant and equipment 
(PPE) during the year.  
 
(ii) 
What assets comprise the RM35.2 million investment properties balance 
transferred from PPE during FY2026? Were these assets reclassified as part 

of a deliberate change in use, and if so, what was the basis of this decision? 
In addition, what is the current utilisation and income-generating status? 
 
(Adapted from company annual report; emphasis added) 
 
(iii) 
What is the group’s target capital structure and financing mix? How does the 
secured revolving credit facility, with relatively high interest rates of 8.45%, 
fit within this strategy? Why is management using revolving credit facilities 
to fund development given that projects have long cash-conversion cycles?

The company was listed on the Catalist board in 2017 and transferred to the SGX 
mainboard in 2021.  
 
(Source: https://sg.finance.yahoo.com/quote/1F3.SI/) 
 
(i) 
What has been the company’s total shareholder return since its transfer to 
the SGX mainboard in 2021 and since its listing in 2017? 

In the sustainability report, the company states that “[the group] recognises the crucial role 
of economic sustainability in balancing growth, financial performance and responsible 
business practices”. 
 
 
(Source: company annual report; emphasis added)  
 
However, over the past three financial years, total economic value distributed has exceeded 
economic value generated. In two of those years, operating costs alone exceeded revenue. 
The economic value distributed to providers of capital was also nil throughout this period.  
 
(ii) 
How does the board reconcile these figures with the company's stated 
commitment to economic sustainability, particularly when operating costs 
have exceeded revenue in two of the three years and providers of capital 
have received no economic value? What guidance has the board given to 
management on providing returns to capital providers in the form of 
dividends?  
 
(iii) 
How have the independent directors assessed management's performance 
over the past decade, particularly in light of the group's financial and 
shareholder return record? 
 
(iv) 
Separately, rather than relying solely on the president and CEO's message 
to shareholders, will the independent chairman provide a regular 
statement to shareholders in the annual report, setting out his assessment 
of the company's performance and prospects, challenges, board 
effectiveness and key governance priorities?

qa.question:
In the joint message to shareholders, the use of drones is identified as a key strategic 
priority. Management expects this technology to improve operational efficiency and reduce 
manpower costs over time, complementing the group’s broader productivity initiatives. The 
group has also developed an AI-enabled robotic workforce, including indoor painting robots 
and drones for facade inspection and washing. 
  
(i) 
Can management elaborate on the extent to which the group deploys its 
painting robots, facade inspection drones and washing drones? What 
proportion of relevant projects uses these technologies, and what 
measurable improvements have they delivered in manpower costs, 
productivity, project completion time and operating margins compared 
with conventional methods? 
 
The share placement and convertible bond agreements were completed in September 2025, 
raising approximately $10.0 million in net proceeds. Almost 60% of these proceeds was 
earmarked for drone development and commercialisation. 
 
(Source: company annual report)  
 
(ii) 
How 
much 
has 
the 
group 
spent 
on 
drone 
development 
and 
commercialisation 
to 
date, 
including 
research 
and 
development, 
equipment, software, staffing and other related costs? What is the total 
investment budget approved by the board for drone-related development? 
 
(iii) 
Given the uncertainty around adoption, scalability and commercialisation, 
what evidence supports the group’s continued investment, and what are the 
principal risks that could undermine the business case? 
 
(iv) 
What aspects of the group’s drone technology are proprietary, and what 
prevents competitors from replicating its capabilities or offering similar 
solutions at lower cost?

Would the board and management provide greater clarity on the following operational 
and financial matters?  

(i) 
Growth: Following the recovery from the pandemic, revenue has declined for two 
consecutive years. What are the principal factors behind this trend, and 
which constraints does management consider most significant to future 
growth, including market demand, pricing, competition, project execution 
and manpower availability?  
 
(Source: company annual report) 
 
Across the repairs and redecoration (R&R), addition and alteration (A&A), 
and coating and painting (C&P) segments, what are the three most 
promising growth opportunities in each segment over the next 18-24 
months, and how does the group intend to pursue them? 
 
(ii) 
Finance costs: Finance costs increased by 13% in FY2026 despite lower revenue. 
In particular, interest on term loans increased by 27.6% even with the repayment 
of a term loan carrying an interest rate of 10%.  
(Source: company annual report) 

What explains this increase in finance costs relating to term loan(s) in 
FY2026, including changes in average borrowings, interest rates, and fees? 
Could management also explain why it accepted the 10% term loan, what 
alternative financing options were considered, and why was this facility 
preferred? 
 
(iii) 
Financing or funding strategy: What capital structure does the board 
consider optimal for the company, taking into account its operating cash 
flow, working capital needs, growth plans and capacity to service debt? 
What roles do short-tenure commercial paper, convertible bonds with 
derivative components, term loans and equity issuance play in the group’s 
funding strategy, and how does management assess their respective costs, 
refinancing risks and potential dilution?

As disclosed in the joint message to shareholders, the group maintains healthy revenue 
visibility, with an order book of approximately $185.3 million as at 1 July 2026, that is 
expected to be progressively delivered over the next two to three years.  
 
On 16 January 2026, SGX RegCo issued a Regulator’s Column1 on forward guidance, in which 
the regulator strongly encouraged issuers to provide meaningful forward-looking 
disclosures. 
 
The Regulator’s Column can be accessed here: 
https://www.sgxgroup.com/media-centre/20260116-regulators-column-forward-
guidance-why-it-matters-and-how-get-it 
 
(i) 
Given SGX RegCo’s encouragement of forward guidance and its view that 
such disclosures can enhance investor confidence and credibility, has the 
board considered providing forward guidance for FY26/27 on the group’s 
performance, outlook, key operating assumptions, and strategic priorities? 
If not, why not? 
 
 
 
1 SGX RegCo noted that forward-looking information consistently ranks highly among the information 
sought by investors, including institutional investors and research analysts, particularly regarding 
anticipated earnings and management’s strategy for achieving those outcomes. The regulator also 
clarified that forward guidance does not require auditor sign-off and that issuers are not expected to 
update guidance immediately for every change in circumstances. Issuers should nevertheless make timely 
announcements in accordance with existing listing rules relating to material information and price-
sensitive developments. 
 
SGX RegCo also highlighted that forward guidance should be viewed as a means for companies to signal 
confidence, build credibility with investors, and potentially support long-term shareholder value, rather 
than as a compliance exercise.

qa.question:
Ms Kemmy Tan was appointed executive director and chief executive officer (CEO) of 
the manager on 1 July 2026, succeeding the former CEO who had been in the role for more 
than 16 years.  
 
The profile of the executive director and CEO is set out on pages 19 and 22 of the annual 
report.  
 
(i) 
What were the key criteria used by the board when selecting a new CEO? In 
particular, how did the board assess the importance of retail industry 
experience, 
investment 
and 
asset-management 
track 
record, 
understanding of REITs, capital allocation capabilities and other skills that 
it considers critical to leading the manager and repositioning the REIT for 
its next phase of growth? 
 
No performance fee was earned by the manager for the year ended 30 June 2026, as the 
performance of the Trust Index was approximately 75% below the benchmark index as at 
30 June 2026. As at 30 June 2015, the underperformance was approximately 1%. This 
represents a significant deterioration in relative performance over the past decade.  
 
(ii) 
What are the three most important changes that the new CEO intends to 
make to the REIT’s strategy or operating model, based on her assessment of 
the factors behind the REIT’s past performance? 
 
(iii) 
Given the REIT’s current size, discount to NAV and acquisition capacity, what 
are the realistic avenues for growth? Which growth opportunities or 
strategic initiatives will be priorities for the new CEO?

Excluding the impact of the divestment of the Wisma Atria office strata units, the 
portfolio valuation would have increased by 0.2% year-on-year. However, the reported fair 
value movements across the portfolio were significantly affected by foreign exchange 
movements. In particular, the Australia Properties1 increased in Singapore dollar terms by 
S$4.2 million despite a decline in Australian dollar terms (down A$21.2 million) and the 
Malaysia Properties showed a significant positive change (5.1% or S$21.3 million) despite a 
RM1 million valuation decline.  
 
 
1 The combined valuation of the Australia Properties was S$336.1 million (A$377.5 million) as at 30 June 
2026, increasing by S$4.2 million from a year ago mainly due to the appreciation of the Australian dollar 
against Singapore dollar. In Australian dollar terms, the valuation declined by A$21.2 million across both 
Adelaide and Perth properties, primarily due to lower income assumptions for Myer Centre Adelaide 
following the unmaterialised activation of Level 5 and softer market rent assumptions. 

(Source: annual report) 
 
(i) 
Foreign exchange effects: Would the board consider providing property 
valuations and year-on-year valuation movements of each property in both 
Singapore dollar and local currency terms in future annual reports and 
presentations? This would allow unitholders to distinguish changes in 
underlying property value from movements arising from foreign exchange. 
 
(ii) 
Myer Centre Adelaide: Myer currently occupies approximately 324,000 square 
feet in the property. Following the arbitration in which Myer’s claim for a 
declaration that it was entitled to terminate its lease was dismissed, what is 
the current working relationship between the manager and Myer? Given 
that the lease expires in 2032 and Myer contributed approximately 7.7% of 
the REIT’s total revenue as at 30 June 2026, what is the board’s assessment 
of the key risks to the income stream over the remaining lease term, and 
after? If Myer were ultimately to exit, what is the current assessment of the 
asset’s repositioning requirements, potential downtime and capital 
expenditure? 
 
(iii) 
Markor: A new tenant, 成都二十四城装饰工程有限公司,commenced its lease in 
the Chengdu property in March 2026, following the departure of Markor 
International Home Furnishings Co., Ltd. Could the manager clarify when 
Markor ceased making rental payments, the total rental arrears 
outstanding at the time of its departure, and the recovery actions taken? 
Revenue from the China Property was reported to be $1.5 million in FY2026, 
compared with $1.6 million in each of FY2025 and FY2024. To what extent did 
the reported rental income in these years translate into cash collections, 

and how much remained uncollected from Markor? Of the $1.45 million 
impairment loss recognised in FY2026, how much related to Markor's 
outstanding receivables? What specific operating and financial milestones 
will the manager use to assess whether the new tenancy has stabilised the 
asset? What has been the level of board oversight relating to matters 
concerning Markor over the past 24 months?  
 
(iv) 
China: The carrying value of the China Property2 has fallen to $9.5 million, from 
$22.2 million in FY2025 and $24.7 million in FY2024, while the remaining lease 
term has shortened to approximately nine years. Could the board explain the 
57% valuation decline between FY2025 and FY2026, including the 
respective impact of the shorter lease term (by just one year), changes in 
passing or market rent, capitalisation or discount rates, and any other 
material valuation assumptions? Given that, in FY2025, the gross revenue 
was $1.6 million, with around 10 years remaining on its lease at that time, 
on what basis did the audit committee satisfy itself that the $22.2 million 
valuation was reasonable and supportable?

According to SGX StockFacts, the REIT trades at approximately a one-third discount to 
its book value of $0.71 per unit. Return on assets and return on equity were 1.58% and 
2.58%, respectively.  
 
 
2 Leasehold estate of 40 years, expiring on 27 December 2035 

(Source: https://investors.sgx.com/market/securities?code=P40U&type=reits&lang=en) 
 
(i) 
Is the board regularly monitoring the REIT’s cost of capital? What is the 
current average weighted cost of capital, and how does the board assess the 
adequacy of the REIT’s 1.58% return on assets and 2.58% return on equity 
relative to that cost? 
 
(ii) 
Has the board undertaken a detailed assessment of the factors contributing 
to the REIT’s substantial discount to book value? What specific measures 
has the board asked management to pursue to address the discount and 
improve value for unitholders, including in the context of the initiatives 
introduced by the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s Equities Market 
Review Group? 
 
At the AGM, the board is seeking unitholder approval on a general mandate to issue new 
units, but is not proposing a unit buyback mandate. 
 
(iii) 
Has the board considered repurchasing units? If so, why is a unit buyback 
mandate not being proposed at the AGM? How does the board compare the 

potential risk-adjusted return from buying back units at a discount of more 
than 30% with the expected returns from deploying capital into 
acquisitions or AEIs?

qa.question:
Despite a 24% increase in revenue in FY2026, profit before tax fell 57% to $13.3 million 
as gross profit decreased from $80.2 million to $68.7 million, largely due to lower margins 
in the cable and wire (C&W) segment, after the provision for onerous contracts.  
(Source: company annual report) 
 
While C&W segment revenue increased by 11.9%, from $343.3 million to $384.1 million, 
segment results fell sharply from $28.5 million to just $7.0 million, reflecting the impact of 
provisions for onerous contracts. 
 
As highlighted in the key audit matter 1 (KAM), the group enters into fixed-price sales 
contracts for cable deliveries. Its gross margins are exposed to fluctuations in copper prices 
because manufacturing costs can rise while contracted selling prices remain unchanged. As 
at 30 June 2026, prevailing copper prices exceeded the fixed selling prices under certain 
contracts with deliveries scheduled over the following one to three and a half years. The 
group consequently recognised an onerous contract provision of $23.89 million, compared 
with $0.76 million in FY2025. 
 
(i) 
Given the volatility of copper prices and delivery periods of up to three and 
a half years, what commercial rationale supported accepting these fixed-
price contracts, and what protections were in place against rising input 
costs? At the point of contract award, what minimum gross margins and 
 
1 The “provision for onerous contracts” is a key audit matter highlighted by the independent auditor. Key 
audit matters are those matters that, in the professional judgement of the independent auditor, were of most 
significance in the audit of the financial statements of the current period. 

copper-price assumptions were used to assess profitability, and how did 
these assumptions compare with actual outcomes? 
 
(ii) 
Has management considered incorporating copper-price pass-through 
clauses, shorter pricing validity periods or other contractual safeguards 
into orders? If these protections are not commercially feasible, how does the 
group price the commodity price risk?  
 
(iii) 
What specific hedging strategy does the group use to manage copper-price 
exposure arising from committed sales orders, and to what extent did this 
strategy mitigate the impact of copper-price movements in FY2026? What 
explains the substantial increase in onerous contract provisions despite the 
use of copper derivatives, and what oversight does the board exercise over 
these exposures and the effectiveness of the hedging strategy? 
 
Furthermore, in Note 10 (Derivative financial instruments; page 130), the company 
disclosed the following:  
 
As at 30 June 2026 and 30 June 2025, the group and the company had outstanding 
copper contracts that were used to hedge significant future fluctuations in copper 
prices. The fair value liabilities of copper contracts for the group was [sic] $976,000 (30 
June 2025: fair value assets of $283,000). The company had no outstanding copper 
contracts as at 30 June 2026 (30 June 2025: fair value asset of $340,000)… 
 
(iv) 
Given that the group’s copper derivatives had a net fair value liability of 
$976,000 as at 30 June 2026, does this indicate that the group held net short 
positions in copper or did it enter into the contract when copper hit a high? 
What underlying exposure were these positions intended to hedge, and how 
did management determine the appropriate direction and size of the 
contracts? 
 
(v) 
What control does the board have in place to ensure that copper derivatives 
are used solely to hedge identifiable business exposures and are not 
speculative in nature?

The group established its renewable energy solutions (RES) business segment through 
the acquisition2 of solar distribution businesses in Thailand and the Philippines, with the aim 
of capturing growing demand for renewable energy. 
 
 
2 On 3 November 2025, the company, together with its wholly-owned subsidiary, Tai Sin (Vietnam) Pte 
Ltd, completed the acquisition of the entire issued share capital of each of Integra R.E. Co., Ltd. (formerly 
known as BayWa r.e. Solar Systems Co., Ltd) (IRECL) and Integra R.E. Corporation (formerly known as 
BayWa r.e. Solar Systems Corporation) (IREC) for an aggregate consideration of $7.341 million. 

The acquisitions of Integra R.E. Co., Ltd. (IRECL) and Integra R.E. Corporation  (IREC) 
resulted in a bargain purchase gain of $4.03 million, representing the excess of the fair value 
of the identifiable net assets acquired over the consideration transferred. The seller disposed 
of the businesses as part of a broader strategic transformation to shift away from pure 
trading activities towards higher value-added manufacturing and project-based businesses. 
IRECL and IREC had been marketed for sale since September 2024. 
 
(i) 
Given that the seller sought to exit these businesses because of their pure 
trading nature, what steady-state return on invested capital does 
management expect IRECL and IREC to generate, and how does this compare 
with the group’s cost of capital? What are the key assumptions 
underpinning these return expectations, including revenue growth, gross 
margins, working capital requirements and customer credit terms? 
 
(ii) 
What competitive advantages do IRECL and IREC have in their respective 
markets that would enable them to sustain margins and defend their 
market positions against competing solar distributors?  
 
In addition, as disclosed in Note 40 (Acquisition of subsidiaries; page 170), IRECL’s acquired 
financial assets included trade receivables with a fair value of $6.118 million and a gross 
contractual value of $6.228 million. 
 
(iii) 
As at the latest available date, how much of the acquired trade receivables 
has been collected, and what proportion remains outstanding? What is the 
ageing profile for the outstanding balance and are any receivables disputed 
or impaired? How do actual collections compare with the assumptions used 
in determining the fair value of these receivables at the acquisition date?

The group’s sustainability report is set out on pages 17 to 52 of the annual report. The 
board oversees sustainability through a sustainability committee comprising the group CEO, 
group CFO and business segment heads.  
 
(i) 
Beyond its quarterly review of sustainability matters at board meetings, 
how does the board actively drive sustainability across the group? What 
specific actions has it taken to ensure that sustainability priorities influence 
business decisions, capital allocation and operational performance? Are 
sustainability targets incorporated into the performance assessments or 
remuneration of senior management? 
  
In addition, it was disclosed that the board approves targets related to the group’s material 
topics. Some examples of these include:  
 
- 
Energy consumption [GRI 302-1]: The group will continue to monitor energy 
consumption across its operations and pursue practical energy efficiency initiatives, 
including further electrification where feasible and improved tracking of electricity, 
fuel and renewable energy usage.  

- 
Employment [GRI 2-7 | 401-1]: The group aims to improve employee retention by 
providing upgrading opportunities that strengthen employee skills and support 
career advancement within the group. 
 
- 
Economic performance [GRI 201-1]: The group aims to achieve long-term sustainable 
growth and to increase shareholder value subject to market conditions. 
 
Some of these targets appear largely qualitative and do not specify measurable outcomes or 
timelines. 
 
(ii) 
Will the board consider committing to translating broad, qualitative 
sustainability commitments into specific, quantifiable and time-bound 
targets for each material topic, supported by established baselines and 
clearly defined performance indicators? By when does the board expect to 
finalise and disclose these targets?
